objectives: Reason about when to use static vs interactive prototypes.

slides.title: Fidelity spectrum + when to use each
slides.body:
**Wireframe / low-fidelity prototype**: rough sketch focusing on layout + structure. No detailed visual design.
- **Hand sketches** (pencil + paper): fastest, cheapest, throwaway.
- **Whiteboard**: collaborative.
- **Low-fi digital** (Balsamiq, Figma sketch-mode): looks intentionally crude. Conveys 'this is rough'.

**Mid-fidelity**: more detailed wireframes with grid + spacing + real labels. No visual design polish.

**High-fidelity / mockup**: full visual design — colors, type, imagery, spacing as it will appear in product.

**Interactive prototype**: clickable; users can navigate through flows. Built in Figma (with prototyping mode), Framer, Protopie, or actual code.

**When to use what**:
- **Idea exploration**: low-fi sketch. Throw 10 directions at the wall.
- **Stakeholder review**: mid-fi (avoid pixel-perfect that gets debates on colors before structure is right).
- **User testing**: ideally hi-fi interactive. Looks like the real product. Behavior matches what user will encounter.
- **Handoff to dev**: hi-fi mockups with annotations, design specs, design tokens.

**Anti-pattern**: prematurely polishing visuals. Spending hours picking colors for a button when the underlying flow doesn't work yet.

**Iterate at the right fidelity**: low-fi is cheap to discard. Hi-fi is expensive — you're attached to it.

**Sketch-Crit-Iterate loop** (popularized by IDEO, Google Design Sprint): 5-day cycle of sketching variations, critiquing, narrowing, prototyping, testing. Aimed at avoiding sunk-cost-on-bad-direction.

slides.title: Figma workflow
slides.body:
**Figma** has become the dominant UI design tool (2020s). Web-based, multi-player real-time editing, plugin ecosystem.

**Files + organization**:
- Files contain pages.
- Pages contain frames (artboards) + components.
- Teams organize files into projects.

**Components**: reusable UI elements. Master component + instances. Update master → all instances update.

**Component properties** (variants): instances vary by properties (size, state, theme). E.g., Button component has variants: Primary/Secondary/Tertiary × Default/Hover/Disabled.

**Auto-layout**: dynamic resizing + stacking. Like CSS flexbox. Resize content + the container adjusts.

**Constraints**: how elements respond to parent resizing. Pin-to-edge, center, stretch.

**Styles**: shared text styles, color styles, effect styles. Update style → all uses update.

**Plugins**: extend Figma. Stark (accessibility), Iconify (icons), Image8 (image generation), Tokens Studio (design tokens). Hundreds available.

**FigJam**: companion whiteboard tool. Used for ideation + workshops.

**Dev mode**: feature for handoff to developers. Inspect spacings, colors, code snippets (HTML, iOS, Android). Generates CSS from design.

**Best practices**:
- Use **components** religiously. Avoid one-off styling.
- Use **auto-layout** for dynamic content (lists, forms).
- Define **design tokens** in styles (colors, type, spacing). Used by code.
- Use **frames + pages** to organize large projects.
- Use **PROTOTYPING MODE** for interactive flows (link frame-to-frame on click).
- **Comments + handoff annotations** for stakeholder + dev review.

**Alternatives**: Sketch (Mac-only, pre-Figma), Adobe XD (struggling), Framer (newer, code-friendly), Penpot (open-source).

slides.title: Interactive prototyping + handoff
slides.body:
Interactive prototype DEMONSTRATES the flow without writing code.

**Figma prototype mode**:
- Connect frames via 'On click' triggers.
- Animation transitions (push, slide, dissolve).
- Conditional logic (limited).
- Smart Animate: auto-tween between similar elements (great for sliders, expanding panels).
- Hover interactions, drag interactions.

**Limits of Figma prototypes**:
- No actual data (text is static).
- No real input (forms can't validate).
- Limited conditional logic.
- Doesn't reflect real performance.

For more complex prototypes:
- **Framer**: closer to actual web. Code components. Real input. Animations.
- **ProtoPie**: complex interactions (sensors on mobile, multi-device).
- **Build in real code** (React, Swift, Vue): for very specific interactions or feedback that matters. Throwaway code; not for production.

**Handoff to dev**:
- **Design tokens** define colors, type, spacing as named variables. Code references the same tokens.
- **Component specs**: which states a component has, props, behavior.
- **Annotations**: 'on click, show modal X with these fields' — written instructions for non-obvious behavior.
- **Asset export**: icons + images in SVG / PNG / WebP. Multiple resolutions for mobile (1x, 2x, 3x).
- **Dev mode tools**: Figma Dev Mode, Zeplin, Avocode generate CSS / iOS / Android snippets directly from designs.

**Design-dev collaboration**:
- **Design reviews**: walkthrough with dev to find feasibility issues early.
- **Design QA**: dev implements, designer checks pixel-by-pixel. Catches gaps.
- **Storybook**: live component library in code. Both designer + dev see the same source of truth.
- **Design systems**: organize tokens + components into a shared library used across products.

question.question: Choose fidelity for a usability test
question.goal: You want to validate a new onboarding flow. Concept: 4 screens. Decide fidelity for user testing.

steps.prompt: Low-fi (paper sketches): users may not take it seriously; can't test visual hierarchy or affordances. Useful for very early concept testing. Pros + cons?

options: Pros: fast iteration; users free to imagine; focuses on structure. Cons: hard to test visual details (button looks like text? color contrast?); users may invent functionality that doesn't exist in real product.

steps.reveal: Low-fi: great for early concept testing; bad for usability validation that depends on visual signal.

steps.prompt: Hi-fi static (Figma mockups, non-interactive): users CAN read screens but can't click through. Pros + cons?

options: Pros: looks real, tests visual hierarchy + readability. Cons: users can't actually interact, so behavior + delight + transitions can't be evaluated.

steps.reveal: Hi-fi static: tests visual but not interactive behavior. Useful for design reviews; insufficient for usability tests.

steps.prompt: Hi-fi interactive (Figma prototyping, clickable): users can navigate. Pros + cons?

options: Pros: tests both visual + interaction; behavior; flow; closest to real product. Cons: takes more time to build; some interactions (real input, error states) still can't be fully tested.

steps.reveal: Hi-fi interactive: standard for usability tests. Closest to real product without writing code. Build the 'happy path' first; add error states + variations as needed.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Fidelity match the question being asked}}$$ Early-concept exploration → low-fi. Visual review → hi-fi static. Usability test → hi-fi interactive. Production-quality testing (performance, real data) → built in code. Choosing the wrong fidelity wastes time (too much polish on a bad idea) or makes results unreliable (paper prototype doesn't reveal visual problems). Match the fidelity to the question.

question.question: Figma's component variants feature lets you:
options: Define one master component with VARIANT PROPERTIES (e.g., Button: size=small/medium/large × state=default/hover/disabled). Instances swap variants without re-creating elements. Updates to master propagate.
question.explanation: Component variants = component states + sizes as a matrix. Define once, instances pick a variant. Updates to master (e.g., redesigned button) update all variants + all instances automatically. Foundational to design systems. Without variants: dozens of separate components for each state, painful to maintain. With variants: clean component library that scales.

slides.workedSolution: Variants: encode state + size as PROPERTIES rather than separate components. Without variants: dozens of buttons (PrimaryDefault, PrimaryHover, PrimaryDisabled, SecondaryDefault, ...). Updates require N edits. With variants: one Button component, instances pick state. Updates propagate. Design system rolls out faster + stays consistent.

question.question: A button component with 3 sizes × 4 states × 2 themes (light/dark). How many distinct variants?
Smooth design-to-dev handoff
question.prompt: Your dev team complains designs change after they start building. Walk through process improvements (design system, tokens, design reviews) that reduce churn.
Explain in two or three sentences why interactive prototypes are essential for usability testing but static mockups suffice for stakeholder review.
question.rubric: Mentions that stakeholders evaluate visual quality + content; users (in usability tests) need to actually navigate + interact to reveal flow issues; static mockups can't test 'where do I click?' or 'how does this transition?' questions. Different tools for different research questions; building hi-fi interactive when only static is needed wastes effort.
